Why violent protests are sweeping across Europe over living costs (CNBC)
What you need to know about Europe's protests, and why they're growing (ABC News)

chunks.text: On October 17, 2026, about 550,000 people {{turned out}} for marches across France, according to news reports. Most of them marched [[peacefully]]. But violence {{broke out}} in Paris and other cities, and some shops were [[looted]]. Officials say about 2,500 people were arrested. On October 19, French authorities {{brought in}} night [[curfews]] in parts of Paris and other cities.

verbs.correct: To be present at an event
verbs.why: Thousands of fans turn out for the big game every year. Few people turn out for town meetings when it rains. About 550,000 people turned out for marches across France on October 17, 2026.
Arguments often break out when people are tired and hungry. A fire sometimes breaks out when someone leaves the stove on. Violence broke out in Paris and other French cities.

verbs.correct: To start using a new rule
verbs.why: Many schools bring in new rules at the start of the year. Some cities bring in higher parking fees in the summer. On October 19, French authorities brought in night curfews in parts of Paris.

chunks.text: The French protests {{grew out of}} a student movement for better schools that began in September 2026. Since then, the anger has {{spilled over}} into wider worries about the [[cost of living]] and [[public services]]. [[Consumer prices]] in September were 3.1 percent higher than a year earlier, according to the national statistics office. Between April and June, the [[unemployment rate]] for people aged 15 to 24 was 21.6 percent. An economist says many governments have {{built up}} huge [[debts]] and cannot easily spend more.

verbs.correct: To begin as a result of something
verbs.wrong: To be banned by the courts
verbs.why: Many big companies grow out of small home businesses. Good friendships often grow out of shared work. The French protests grew out of a student movement that began in September 2026.

verbs.correct: To spread to include more things
verbs.wrong: To be shared on social media
verbs.why: Stress at work often spills over into family life. Problems at one school sometimes spill over into the whole town. In France, the anger has spilled over into wider worries about the cost of living.

verbs.correct: To slowly gather a large amount
verbs.why: Dust builds up fast in an empty house. Some students build up large debts during college. An economist says many governments have built up huge debts.

chunks.text: Similar protests have {{sprung up}} elsewhere in Europe. In Spain and Portugal, people are angry about high [[rent]] and housing costs. Spain will hold an [[early election]] on November 29. In Italy, some marches over living costs ended in [[clashes]] with police. On October 20, Italy's government said it will send 500 soldiers to Milan. It also plans to {{crack down}} on [[youth gangs]]. [[Opposition politicians]] say the government does little about housing.

verbs.correct: To appear quickly in many places
verbs.why: New coffee shops spring up all over the city. Food stands spring up near the stadium before every game. Similar protests have sprung up in Spain, Portugal and Italy.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To give money to young people
verbs.why: The city cracks down on drivers who park in bus lanes. Schools crack down on cheating during final exams. Italy's government plans to crack down on youth gangs after the protests in Milan.

chunks.text: President Emmanuel Macron [[condemned]] the violence. He blamed radical left-wing groups for taking control of a movement with real [[concerns]]. A left-wing party leader rejected the claim. France will {{set aside}} money to help damaged areas [[recover]]. The governments of Italy and Belgium have also condemned the violence and have not {{backed down}}. Officials say the violence in France {{died down}} on the night of October 19. But more marches are planned for Saturday, October 24, and France will {{step up}} its [[police presence]].

verbs.correct: To keep money for a special use
verbs.wrong: To ask other countries for money
verbs.why: She sets aside some money every month for her vacation. Many parents set aside money for their children's college. France's government will set aside money to help damaged areas recover.

verbs.correct: To agree to what others demand
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to decide
verbs.why: The company sometimes backs down when workers threaten to strike. My father rarely backs down once he makes a decision. Italy and Belgium have not backed down after the protests.
The wind usually dies down at night. The noise dies down when the concert ends. Officials say the violence in France died down on the night of October 19.

verbs.correct: To increase the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To move police to the border
verbs.why: Stores step up security in December. Police step up patrols during big festivals. France will step up its police presence for the marches on October 24.

vocab.def: To be present at an event
ex: Hundreds of people turned out for the free concert in the park.
Not many voters turned out because of the snowstorm.
Will enough parents turn out for the school meeting?
A fight broke out in the parking lot after the game.
Panic broke out when the fire alarm rang.
A thunderstorm broke out just as our picnic started.

vocab.def: To start using a new rule
ex: Our school brought in a new dress code this fall.
Many states have brought in laws against texting while driving.
The city plans to bring in a new parking rule next year.

vocab.def: To begin as a result of something
ex: The company grew out of a small garage business.
Her book grew out of letters she wrote to her son.
The festival grew out of a small neighborhood party.

vocab.def: To spread to include more things
ex: His bad mood at work spilled over into the weekend.
The argument spilled over into the next meeting.
Money problems often spill over into other parts of life.

vocab.def: To slowly gather a large amount
ex: He built up a lot of credit card debt in college.
Snow built up on the roof all week.
She slowly built up her savings over ten years.

vocab.def: To appear quickly in many places
ex: Pizza places have sprung up all over our neighborhood.
Small towns sprang up along the new railroad.
New apartment buildings are springing up near the river.

vocab.def: To act strongly to stop something
ex: The police are cracking down on speeding near schools.
Our school cracked down on cell phones in class.
The state wants to crack down on fake online reviews.

vocab.def: To keep money for a special use
ex: I set aside 50 dollars a week for groceries.
The town set aside money to repair the old bridge.
Try to set aside a little money for emergencies.

vocab.def: To agree to what others demand
ex: The landlord backed down and lowered the rent.
After weeks of pressure, the coach finally backed down.
The store refused to back down on the price.
The rain died down by the afternoon.
We waited for the cheering to die down.
The excitement about the new phone died down quickly.

vocab.def: To increase the amount of something
ex: The airport stepped up security checks before the long weekend.
Our team needs to step up its training before the final.
The city stepped up trash pickup after the festival.

wordDefs.def: In a calm way, without fighting or violence
ex: The two neighbors settled their argument peacefully.
The crowd waited peacefully outside the stadium.
The children played peacefully in the yard.

wordDefs.def: Robbed during a time of disorder, often by a crowd
ex: Several stores were looted after the hurricane.
The museum was looted during the war.
Police guarded the mall so it would not be looted.

wordDefs.def: Rules that say people must not be in public places at certain hours
ex: Some towns have curfews for teenagers on school nights.
The army ordered curfews after the earthquake.
Many parents set curfews for their children.

wordDefs.def: The amount of money people need for food, housing and other basic needs
ex: The cost of living in big cities is very high.
She moved to a small town with a lower cost of living.
Pay raises often do not match the cost of living.

wordDefs.def: Services such as schools, hospitals and buses that a government pays for
ex: Taxes help pay for public services.
Many people in rural areas have poor public services.
The mayor promised to improve public services.

wordDefs.def: The prices that people pay for everyday goods and services
ex: Consumer prices usually rise when gas gets more expensive.
The bank watches consumer prices every month.
Lower consumer prices helped families save money.

wordDefs.def: The share of people who want a job but cannot find one
ex: The unemployment rate fell to 4 percent in June.
Our state has a lower unemployment rate than its neighbors.
A high unemployment rate is hard on young workers.

wordDefs.def: Money that a person, company or country owes
ex: They paid all their debts before buying a house.
Medical bills left the family with large debts.
The company sold buildings to pay its debts.

wordDefs.def: Money you pay each month to live in a home that someone else owns
ex: My rent rose by 100 dollars this year.
She pays her rent on the first day of each month.
Rent is cheaper outside the city.

wordDefs.def: A vote held before the normal date, often after a political problem
ex: The leader called an early election to get more support.
An early election gives parties little time to prepare.
Many voters were surprised by the early election.

wordDefs.def: Short, violent fights between two groups
ex: There were clashes between rival fans after the match.
The clashes lasted for several hours.
Police tried to stop clashes near the border.

wordDefs.def: Groups of young people who often commit crimes together
ex: The city started a sports program to protect kids from youth gangs.
Youth gangs were a big problem in the neighborhood.
Teachers worry about youth gangs near the school.

wordDefs.def: Politicians from parties that are not in the government
ex: Opposition politicians voted against the new tax.
The plan was criticized by opposition politicians.
Opposition politicians asked the minister to explain the delay.

wordDefs.def: Said in public that something is very wrong
ex: World leaders condemned the attack.
The school condemned the bullying in a letter to parents.
The team condemned the fans' bad behavior.
Parents raised concerns about safety at the school.
The doctor listened to all my concerns.
There are concerns about the cost of the new stadium.

wordDefs.def: To return to a normal or good condition
ex: The town needed years to recover from the flood.
Small businesses slowly recover after hard times.
The economy began to recover in the spring.

wordDefs.def: The number of police officers who can be seen in a place
ex: There was a heavy police presence at the parade.
A strong police presence made shoppers feel safe.
The city increased its police presence downtown.

mainIdea.s: Anger about prices, rent and weak public services has led to large marches in several European countries. France ordered curfews after violence, and Italy is sending soldiers to Milan.
mainIdea.why: Protests about the cost of living have sprung up across Europe. French authorities brought in curfews, and Italy plans to crack down after clashes in Milan.

mainIdea.s: Protests over the high cost of everyday life have spread from France to other nations. Most leaders have answered by cutting taxes and promising new money for schools and homes.
mainIdea.why: Close, but governments have condemned the violence and have not backed down. France brought in curfews, and Italy is sending soldiers.

mainIdea.s: The European Union has agreed on a new plan to build cheap apartments for young workers. Member countries will share the cost, and the first homes should be ready in two years.
mainIdea.why: This is about protests that broke out over living costs. Governments answered with curfews, soldiers and plans to step up police.

tf.s: Violence broke out in several French cities during the marches.
tf.why: Most people marched peacefully, but violence broke out in Paris and other cities.

tf.s: Most of the people who turned out in France were violent.
tf.why: About 550,000 people turned out, and most of them marched peacefully.

tf.s: The French protests grew out of a student movement.
tf.why: They began with a student movement for better schools in September 2026.

tf.s: Italy is sending soldiers to Milan after the protests there.
tf.why: Italy's government will send 500 soldiers to Milan, and it plans to crack down on youth gangs.

tf.s: The anger in France is only about the state of schools.
tf.why: It has spilled over into wider worries about the cost of living and public services.

tf.s: Several governments have agreed to all of the protesters' demands.
tf.why: Governments in Italy and Belgium have condemned the violence and have not backed down.

lines.text: Did you see the news from France? About 550,000 people {{turned out}} for marches on October 17.
I saw that. Most of them were peaceful, right?
Yes, but violence {{broke out}} in some cities. France {{brought in}} night curfews in parts of Paris.
What are people so angry about?
It {{grew out of}} a student movement about schools. Then the anger {{spilled over}} into prices and public services.
I can see why. A lot of families are living [[paycheck to paycheck]].
Young people especially. Jobs are hard to get, and rent is high.
So they get [[the short end of the stick]].
That's how many of them feel. And protests have {{sprung up}} in Spain, Portugal and Italy too.
Anger like that can [[spread like wildfire]].
Italy is sending 500 soldiers to Milan. It also wants to {{crack down}} on youth gangs.
Have any governments given the protesters what they want?
Not really. Italy and Belgium haven't {{backed down}}.
Why don't they just spend more on schools and housing?
Many governments have {{built up}} huge debts, so their budgets are [[stretched thin]].
Still, they can't [[kick the can down the road]] forever.
True. For now, France will {{step up}} its police presence for the marches on October 24.
I hope those marches stay peaceful.

expressions.def: Used to say that people spend all their pay each month and cannot save any
ex: Many young workers live paycheck to paycheck.
We lived paycheck to paycheck when I was a kid.

expressions.expr: the short end of the stick
expressions.def: The worst part of a deal or situation
ex: New workers often get the short end of the stick.
When the budget was cut, our school got the short end of the stick.

expressions.def: To spread very quickly to many people or places
ex: The news spread like wildfire at school.

expressions.def: Used to say that money, time or people must cover too many needs
ex: Our small team is stretched thin this month.
With three kids, our money is stretched thin.

expressions.expr: kick the can down the road
expressions.def: To keep delaying a hard decision or problem
ex: Lawmakers keep kicking the can down the road on the budget.
